To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
chronic clonidine infused in the PVN does increase rather than decrease susceptibility to ABA in the rat.

(1) clonidine infused chronically into the PVN exacerbates rather than ameliorates susceptibility to activity-based (ABA) anorexia; (2) clonidine does not increase food intake; (3) clonidine decreases wheel running; and (4) clonidine increases susceptibility to ABA in the absence of changes in food intake or wheel activity.
clonidine infused in the PVN of the rat increases susceptibility to ABA.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the role of the PVN noradrenergicsystem in the control of feeding and body weight.
the role of the PVN in ABA.
understanding the neurobiological basis of anorexia and bulimia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

chronic PVN infusion of clonidine exacerbates rather than reduces susceptibility to ABA, which is in agreement with our previous findings that PVN noradrenergics are activated rather than reduced in response to ABA.
the noradrenergically mediated feeding response is not mediated by the PVN.
clonidine does not have an effect on food intake and wheel running behavior and exacerbates susceptibility to ABB.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
chronic clonidine infused directly into the PVN increases susceptibility to ABA, and that this effect appears independent of changes in wheel activity and food intake.
the PVN noradrenergics system is not a major regulator of food intake or activity in rats.
PVN alpha 2-adrenoceptors are not involved in the regulation of ABA susceptibility.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the PVN is not a site of action for clonidine to produce hyperphagie and that the PVN may be involved in the pathogenesis of ABA.
clonidine infused in the PVN does NOT attenuate the development of anorexia.
the PVN noradrenergics system does not appear to be involved in the control of ABA.
